title: Ideas vs Judgment and Execution: why picking the right mountain matters
summary: Buchheit argues both "ideas are worthless" and "ideas are valuable" are wrong when stated simply. Using a mountain-climbing metaphor, he shows that value comes from the judgment to pick the right product and route, plus a team able to execute, and that ideas gain value when they come from someone with a track record of being right.

principles.text: Market and product choice matter more than team brilliance: a mediocre team on the right product beats a brilliant team on the wrong one.
principles.quote: A mediocre team building the right product will succeed and a brilliant team building the wrong product will fail.

principles.text: Ideas are plentiful and most are bad; the scarce asset is judgment about which ideas hold real value and a team that can reach it.
principles.quote: Ideas are plentiful. The problem is that most ideas are bad -- either there's no gold at the top of the mountain, or the ascent is too difficult with today's technology.

principles.text: Judgment drives both which product to build and which route to take, including changing course when the current path isn't working.
principles.quote: It also requires good judgment in order to choose the right route, or to change course when you realize that the current path isn't working out.

principles.text: An idea's credibility comes from the person pitching it: someone with a history of being right gets listened to.
principles.quote: The idea has value because it comes from someone who has a history of being right.

principles.text: If you believe in an idea but have no track record, prove it yourself rather than expecting others to buy it.
principles.quote: If that person truly believes in their idea, they will have to prove it on their own.

principles.text: Success is multiplicative: idea, judgment, ability, determination and luck all have to be present.
